snip.t: *Hepatomegaly or right upper quadrant tenderness:* Pyogenic or amoebic liver abscess, acute hepatitis, or congestive hepatopathy from sepsis.
| Amoebic liver abscess | Right upper quadrant pain, tender liver | Ultrasound focal defect, dysenteric stool history |

Ingestion of cysts (contaminated food/water) $\rightarrow$ Excystation in intestine $\rightarrow$ Trophozoites invade colonic mucosa $\rightarrow$ Ulceration, dysentery $\rightarrow$ Haematogenous spread to liver (abscess).
Jaundice: Liver dysfunction (e.g., severe malaria, amoebic liver abscess).
| Pyogenic liver abscess | Biliary disease, older, often multiple | Culture of pus; antibiotics and drainage |

qs.q: A patient with a liver abscess is drained. The aspirate is chocolate-brown and non-purulent. What does this indicate about the nature of the abscess?
o: It represents a pyogenic abscess caused by a secondary bacterial infection.
It represents a fungal abscess containing hyphae and inflammatory cells.
It represents a hydatid cyst containing protoscolices and fluid content.
It represents an amoebic abscess containing necrotic tissue and blood.
It represents a parasitic cyst containing viable larvae and fluid.
qs.e: Amoebic liver abscesses contain necrotic tissue and blood, appearing chocolate-brown.
qs.s: Weekly Year 2: Parasitology Exam - November 13, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: A patient with a liver abscess is treated with metronidazole. The parasite is Entamoeba histolytica. Why is a luminal agent also required?
o: To prevent the systemic spread of the parasite to other vital organs.
To treat the concurrent bacterial infection present within the abscess.
To enhance the systemic absorption of the metronidazole in the liver.
To reduce the severe inflammatory response occurring in the gut wall.
To prevent the recurrence of the infection from residual intestinal cysts.
qs.e: Luminal agents are needed to eliminate residual cysts in the intestine.
qs.s: Weekly Year 2: Parasitology Exam - November 13, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: A patient with a liver abscess is treated with paromomycin. The parasite is Entamoeba histolytica. Why is this drug chosen over metronidazole?
o: Paromomycin achieves higher bioavailability when taken with food.
Paromomycin is associated with fewer gastrointestinal side effects.
Paromomycin has fewer interactions with routine gastrointestinal medicines.
Paromomycin is safer for patients who have underlying liver disease.
Paromomycin is more active against the intestinal cyst stage of Entamoeba.
qs.e: Paromomycin is effective against intestinal cysts, unlike metronidazole.
qs.s: Weekly Year 2: Parasitology Exam - November 13, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: During the therapeutic drainage of a suspected amoebic liver abscess, what distinctive macroscopic appearance is classically expected of the aspirated necrotic material?
o: Anchovy paste-like reddish-brown thick liquid
Bright green purulent fluid with foul odor
Clear serous exudate with occasional blood flecks
Bright yellow creamy pus with high viscosity
Dark black tarry fluid containing digested blood
qs.e: Amebic liver abscess aspiration yields characteristic chocolate-brown or anchovy paste-like necrotic material lacking neutrophils.
qs.s: Weekly Year 2: Parasitology Exam - October 30, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: A patient with a ruptured liver abscess presents with pleuritic chest pain and the expectoration of chocolate-brown sputum. What is the primary anatomical route by which the hepatic lesion tracked to reach the respiratory tract?
o: Direct hematogenous spread via the inferior vena cava
Lymphatic migration through the retroperitoneal space
Direct extension upward through the muscular diaphragm
Aspiration of swallowed gastric contents into trachea
Perforation into the peritoneal cavity followed by ascites
qs.e: Right lobe liver abscesses frequently rupture directly through the diaphragm into the pleural cavity and bronchial tree.
qs.s: Weekly Year 2: Parasitology Exam - October 30, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: When is therapeutic needle aspiration specifically indicated in the management of a suspected amoebic liver abscess?
o: To differentiate amoebic from pyogenic pus
When no response to therapy occurs in days
To prevent the development of effusion
As a routine first-line diagnostic procedure
qs.e: Aspiration is not conventionally required unless there is no response to therapy after 3-5 days or the abscess is at immediate risk of rupture. Routine aspiration is discouraged because medical therapy is highly effective.

qs.q: What is the characteristic macroscopic appearance of the fluid obtained from an aspirated amoebic liver abscess?
o: Bright red bloody hemorrhagic fluid
Foul-smelling purulent green pus fluid
Chocolate-colored anchovy paste fluid
Clear straw-colored transudative fluid
qs.e: The aspirate consists of an acellular proteinaceous debris described as chocolate-colored anchovy paste fluid. Purulent green pus is more typical of pyogenic bacterial abscesses.

qs.q: A patient presents with a suspected amoebic liver abscess. Which of the following laboratory findings is typically present in the peripheral blood?
o: Isolated thrombocytopenia
Pancytopenia presentation
Leucocytosis without eosinophilia
Marked eosinophilia present
qs.e: Peripheral blood testing in hepatic amoebiasis typically demonstrates leucocytosis without eosinophilia. Eosinophilia is characteristic of helminthic infections rather than amoebic liver abscesses.

ai.title: Liver Abscess
ai.subject: Microbiology & immunology
ai.summary: Liver abscesses are focal collections of pus in the liver, most commonly pyogenic or amoebic. Diagnosis relies on history, imaging and, where possible, microbiology. Management is source control plus targeted antibiotics.

sections.p: A liver abscess is a localized collection of necrotic tissue and pus within the hepatic parenchyma. In low‑resource settings the two main etiologies are pyogenic (often Klebsiella pneumoniae, E. coli, or Staphylococcus aureus) and amoebic (Entamoeba histolytica).

Pyogenic organisms are gram‑negative rods or gram‑positive cocci that can be isolated from blood or aspirate. Entamoeba histolytica is a protozoan with a cyst stage that survives in contaminated water and a trophozoite that invades colonic mucosa and spreads hematogenously to the liver.

Pyogenic abscesses arise from biliary tract disease, portal vein seeding, or trauma. Amoebic abscesses result from ingestion of cysts in fecally contaminated food or water, excystation in the ileum, colonic invasion, and hematogenous spread to the liver.

Both types present with fever, right upper quadrant pain, and hepatomegaly. Amoebic abscesses often follow dysentery; pyogenic abscesses may be associated with biliary disease, diabetes or immunosuppression.

History of dysentery, diabetes or biliary disease, fever and RUQ pain. Physical exam: tender hepatomegaly, possible jaundice. Imaging: ultrasound is first line; CT if available. Lab: raised CRP/ESR, leukocytosis. Microbiology: stool antigen or serology for Entamoeba; pus culture for pyogenic.

t.b: Detects hypoechoic lesion, guides aspiration; a positive finding is a focal liver defect with or without internal echoes.
Confirms size, wall thickness, and presence of gas; a positive finding is a well‑defined hypodense area with rim enhancement.
Identifies pyogenic organism; a positive result guides antibiotic choice.
Directly isolates the causative bacteria; a positive result confirms pyogenic etiology.
Detects Entamoeba histolytica antigen; a positive result confirms amoebic abscess.
Detects anti‑Entamoeba antibodies; a positive result supports diagnosis when stool is negative.
